memories.memory_text: I held the battered passport in my hands—my face, my name: Jason Bourne. I said it out loud, over and over, like saying it might make it true. 'Hi, I'm Jason. Jason Bourne. Jason Bourne, nice to meet you.'

I lifted the tray and saw the money—stacks of hundreds, nearly a million dollars—and then the five other passports, all with my face but different names. I kept saying 'My name is Jason Bourne,' but it didn't help. It all felt hollow. Suddenly, it was all fucked up.

I was at the consulate, standing at that window, and she kept asking me if I was a citizen, if I had a passport—simple questions, but I couldn't answer right. My mind was racing, too much noise, too many eyes, and I just had to get out.
I was taking the stairs two or three at a time, pushing up fast, when the alarm started screaming — bleet, bleet, bleet — sudden and sharp, like a trigger pulled behind me.
I reached behind to adjust the bag and felt it slip—then the thud when it hit the courtyard. I couldn't look, but I knew it was gone.
I caught the drainpipe just in time, felt it tearing from the wall, then grabbed the gutter—held just long enough to slow the fall before dropping the last fifteen feet.
I stood by her car and told her I needed a ride, then offered ten thousand dollars to get to Paris—she was angry, scared, but I knew she wouldn’t call the police.
I told her I don't know who I am—I can't remember anything before two weeks ago. I meant it, and I could see she didn't believe me.

I remember sitting in that quiet truckstop cafe, showing Marie all the passports and money from the bank box, and realizing out loud that the things I know how to do—fighting, escaping, scanning for exits—weren't just paranoia, they meant something bad had to have happened to me.
I turned the key and opened the door, expecting something—anything—but there was nothing. No one waiting, no answers, just an empty apartment.

I picked up the frying pan, then the spoon, saying each was mine—this is my frying pan, this is my spoon—trying to make the words stick, make the objects mean something, but they didn’t. The kitchen felt staged, empty, like it belonged to someone else.

I sat at the desk, staring at the binders and books about maritime law, ship schedules, registries—all about boats—and for a second I thought maybe I was in shipping, but it didn’t feel real. It was like reading someone else’s life in a file.
I held the Jason Bourne passport in my hand and watched it burn—my face melting in the flame—until I dropped it just before it seared my skin. I couldn't keep pretending that name was mine.

Marie touched my shoulder and then took my hand—I didn't know how to react—and when she guided it down her body, I froze, unsure if I should let this happen. Then I pulled her in and we kissed, and for the first time in forever, I wanted to feel something real.
I stood in the elevator, in a suit, watching my reflection in the mirrored ceiling—cleaned up, but still coiled tight, every nerve alive.

I was looking through the brochures, trying to piece it together—boats, water, something about the sea—when Marie came back and said she found Kane. She said she found the body. I didn't wait. I stood up. We had to move. That phone was a beacon.
I opened freezer #121 and it was empty—Kane’s body was gone. I just stood there for a second, feeling the weight of it.
I grabbed the sign-in book, pretended I wanted to sign in, then ripped the page out before slamming the morgue boss into the wall and pulling Marie out.
I saw the name Nykwana Wombosi in the Alliance Security brochure and it clicked — same guy who visited the morgue, same yacht, same security package. I knew then it wasn't random.
I told Marie to go back to the hotel. I didn’t look back — I couldn’t slow down. She was scared, but I had to move, alone.
I looked up into the camera, knowing they'd see me — knowing they'd know it was me.
I stood in the streetlight, looking up at the camera, and said it clearly—I'm here, I'm waiting, I know you're watching.
I stood at the gate, took a deep breath, and walked into Wombosi's compound — I knew there was no turning back.

I stood there in front of Wombosi, surrounded by his guards and staring children, and he asked me how it feels to be dead—like he knew something I didn’t, like my face or body had already told him everything.
He slammed a bomb onto the throne and accused me of putting it in his engine room. He said I came to get close, then brought death. I realized then he knew who I really was.
Marie said it doesn't matter who I was — only who I want to be. She said we could leave, go until we couldn't go anymore, and that's who she wants to be.
I turned off the light and took her hand. We lay in the dark without speaking, just breathing, staying still for once.

I kicked open the back door and pulled Marie into the courtyard, hearing the alarm scream as bullets tore through the front of the hotel—I vaulted the wall, hauled her up and over, then turned to fire twice while the rounds shredded the stone beside me.

After reloading on the run, I saw a woman frozen in her kitchen—no time to stop—then spotted the Professor vaulting the wall, blood on his face, forcing us to climb again, leap across walls, slide down a steep roof, and crash into a walled courtyard with an open window ahead.
I remember the Professor saying 'Treadstone... both of us...' and something cracking open in my head — like a name I’d forgotten, like a door I couldn’t push through until then.
I pulled the e-phone pager from his pocket, blood slick on my fingers, and wiped the screen — it hummed, and I knew it. Not from a story, not from a briefing. From me.
I handed Marie the locker key and told her to take it — to get out, get low, stay low. I said I couldn't protect her anymore, and she just looked at me like I was already gone.

memories.memory_text: I told them I paid four thousand dollars—my last four thousand—to a man to marry me, and I admitted he was already married; I showed them Mr. Thomas’s name, I told him everything myself.
I kept saying my address was from two days ago because I lost my apartment, and I had all the papers, but the clerk just kept shutting me down like I was the problem.
I was storming away, furious, tearing that damn parking ticket to pieces and stomping on it—everything was falling apart, I was broke, illegal, ruined.
He just tossed a stack of cash—hundreds—right at me, and I caught it. I looked at the money, then at him, then back at the money, not knowing whether to run or believe this was real.
I was pacing, trying to think, and then he grabbed me—just grabbed me out of nowhere. I froze. He did too. It was like we both couldn't believe it happened.
He said he just wanted a ride to Paris, like we were a couple. I asked if I’d be safe, if I’d get the money—and when he said he wouldn’t hurt me, I knew I had to decide.
I remember the way he said he didn’t know who he was—like it was just a fact—and how my hands tightened on the wheel because suddenly he wasn’t just some cold guy with a bag of cash, he was… lost.
I was so tired of talking about my own mess, I snapped and said, 'Well, this is great. I'm sick of myself and you have no idea who you are,' like his amnesia was just another goddamn inconvenience.

When he started listing all those details—about the cars, the waitress, the truck—I froze. Then I realized he wasn't acting, wasn't making it up. I whispered, 'God, you're not kidding, are you?' because I finally believed him.
He didn’t ask me to come up—he just handed me money, like that’s all I was there for. I took it, but it wasn’t what I wanted.
When he said, 'How could I forget about you? You're the only person I know,' something cracked—like maybe I mattered. I actually smiled.

I held the picture in my hand, glass broken around it, and I just knew — he was dead. I looked at Bourne and said it out loud: 'He's dead, isn't he?' But then it hit me — he already knew. 'You knew he was coming.'
I couldn't breathe — he had my picture, he came for me, and Bourne wouldn't admit it. I backed up inside myself, overwhelmed, and whispered, 'Oh, Jesus...' I didn't know what to believe anymore.
I helped Bourne shove that red bag into the locker—my hands were shaking, but I remember the cold metal of the handle and the way the door slammed shut like it was sealing everything away.
I held out my passport to Bourne, like he did with his—showing him I trusted him, that I was giving something real up, even if he didn’t understand.
When he didn’t take it, I touched his shoulder—then took his hand and guided it down my body, not speaking, just needing to feel something real, something that meant I was still here.
This can't be it — the whole place was empty, wires hanging, carpet torn up, like someone erased everything.
I found Kane. I found the body. It took six calls, and when I finally got the confirmation, my skin crawled — I could feel it, something cold and wrong.
I saw the freezer was empty—Freezer #121—Kane’s body was gone. I remember the attendant pulling it open and just standing there, confused, like he didn’t understand what he was seeing.

I was trying to reach him, asking what he was doing, but he just kept walking, ripping through those brochures like I wasn’t even there — his voice was flat, like he didn’t care if I understood or not.

I asked him what we were doing, and he just said to go back to the hotel — that’s when I stopped, standing there on the street, watching him disappear into the dark, knowing I couldn’t follow anymore.
I told him it doesn't matter who he was before — it's who he wants to be, and I meant it, because when he looked at me, I knew I was ready to go, to leave everything and just keep moving with him.
Bourne grabbed me so hard my arm stung, yanking me up and swinging me over that first wall like I weighed nothing — I barely had time to breathe before I was on the other side, running.

I was sliding down that steep roof, losing my balance, crashing hard into the courtyard below — all while hearing shots behind us, not knowing if we were trapped or if the window ahead was our way out.
I remember asking if we lost them, my voice tight, and when Bourne just shook his head, I had to know — I asked again, 'Who is it?' but he was already moving, like answers didn’t matter.
I was walking fast with Bourne when suddenly he slammed me to the ground behind a car—no warning—just the sound of gunfire tearing everything apart.
I could hear bullets ripping through the street, cops shouting at both ends, and then the Professor opened fire on them—suddenly we were caught in a three-way shootout and Bourne yanked me away.

I was right behind Bourne, running through that cramped shop when the door exploded open and the Professor came through — Bourne froze because there was a woman behind him, and then the shots started tearing through the air.
I was running with Bourne, breath burning in my chest, and then he yanked the car door open for me — I didn’t think, just threw myself inside.
The gunshot cracked, glass exploded in my face — I flinched hard before I even registered the cop, and then Bourne swerved like we were being hunted from both sides.
I saw the Professor gaining on us in the rearview, his gun coming up — I reached for Bourne’s shotgun and shouted, 'Give me the gun —' before grabbing it.
I had the shotgun in my hands, leaning out the window, aiming back at the Professor as Bourne swerved through traffic — I was ready to fire.
I saw the Professor attacking Bourne, and I grabbed the shotgun—my hands were shaking but I fired, I shot him in the back.
After I shot him, Bourne turned to me—I handed him the gun, and he took it without a word, then started reloading.

I took the key from him—cold metal in my palm—and stared at Bourne, jaw tight, refusing to let anything break loose. There was enough in that locker to disappear, to become someone else, but all I could feel was the weight of it cutting me loose.

I asked him 'What about you?' and he didn't answer—not really. Just stood there. So I ran. I didn't look back, but I felt every step echo behind me, like he was still watching, like he was already gone.
I was handing out helmets at the scooter rental when I looked up and saw him standing there—different hair, but that smile… I asked if he had ID, even though I already knew it didn’t matter.
